methods: Rewrite the condition as a congruence on the root modulo a power of ten, lift the solutions from modulo ten to higher powers via Hensel/CRT casework, combine residue classes with the modulus to enumerate solutions in increasing order, then reduce the corresponding quotient modulo the required modulus.

Uniqueness of binary digit determines each x_k from the congruence 7 S_n ≡ 1 mod 2^n; compute successive digits via a recursive reversal rule, then read off the required consecutive digits and evaluate the weighted sum.
Solve N^2 ≡ N mod 10^4, factor the modulus into prime powers, find idempotent residues modulo each prime power, recombine via CRT, and read off the leading three digits.

types.name: Calendar and periodic simultaneous-event counting via overlapping cycles
methods: Convert the date to a day-of-week index, advance by each year's shift (1 plus extra for leap years), and find the first offset congruent to the target weekday, accounting for the century leap rule.
Compute each pairwise coincidence count in the period, subtract twice the triple-coincidence count (and account for endpoints) to get days with exactly two visitors.

Each block spans a fixed-length consecutive interval; count multiples of the divisor per block using periodicity over the common block length, since the divisor divides the block length handle full cycles and remainder.

types.name: Roots of unity, trigonometric sequences, and angle congruences
methods: Translate sign conditions into intervals for the doubled angle mod 180, iterate the doubling map on the interval, intersect the resulting periodic interval constraints to pin down the angle, then convert to degrees.
Write z = e^{iθ}; impose imaginary-part-zero condition, convert to a congruence on θ modulo 2π, count distinct solutions by gcd/lattice argument, reduce mod 1000.

types.name: subset counting with coverage, mandatory, or disjoint-pair constraints via casework/inclusion-exclusion
methods: Enumerate subsets of the grid up to size; count those covering all rows and columns, and count those covering all rows and columns with a redundant element; take the ratio.

List the ordered pairs summing to each target; count four-element subsets containing at least one pair from each target list by partitioning the pair-lists into disjoint groups, then apply inclusion-exclusion over which required pairs are used, subtract overlaps where a single element participates in both sums, and add back cases where the four elements form two required pairs.
Fix the required course, then count the remaining slots by total subsets minus the subsets avoiding the required category.

types.name: inclusion-exclusion over set unions and intersection-region counts
methods: Use inclusion-exclusion for the union and maximize the intersection subject to containment of the smaller set in the larger.

Use inclusion-exclusion on the union of the three talent sets; each "cannot" statement gives a complement count, convert to set sizes, and since the triple intersection is empty solve for the number in exactly two sets.

Apply inclusion-exclusion for three sets; relate the sum of pairwise intersections to the number taking at least two classes by adding twice the triple intersection; solve for the triple intersection.

types.name: ordered factorizations and divisibility chains via recursive divisor/multiset-partition counting
methods: Factor the target, decompose into ratios forming a smooth factorization, and count ordered divisor chains by distributing prime exponents across successive ratio terms.

Define the count by splitting off the first factor greater than one, so the total equals the sum over nontrivial divisors of the count for the complementary quotient, with the empty quotient contributing one; evaluate recursively from the prime factorization.

types.name: digit-string counting under divisibility, base, parity, or digit restrictions via complement and carry casework
methods: Split coefficients by parity of degree, apply the signed evaluation constraint to reduce to an alternating sum, subtract a constant to make all terms nonnegative, then count solutions by stars-and-bars with upper-bound constraints (inclusion-exclusion) over the two sign groups.
Count by digit choices: fix the last digit to be odd and exclude forbidden digits, enforce digit-sum divisible by 3, and subtract/handle the hundreds place being nonzero.

Partition numbers by residue mod 3; use the constraint that adjacent cells must differ by a nonzero residue, determine the forced residue coloring of the grid, count assignments of each residue class to its cells, multiply, then factor and count divisors.

types.name: permutation counting with forbidden adjacencies, positions, or descents via inclusion-exclusion
methods: Count permutations whose increasing-value extraction finishes in exactly two passes using inclusion-exclusion on the number of passes, or by characterizing the descent/block structure.

Count arrangements of all children into a fixed-seat grid, then use inclusion-exclusion over the forbidden conditions (same row adjacent seats, same column front-back) to remove placements where a sibling pair is together.

For each modulus, the condition forces entries at positions differing by the modulus to be congruent mod that modulus; choose residues for each position class consistently (CRT), then count permutations realizing each valid residue assignment and sum all cases.

types.name: permutations and tableaux via interval-growth, linear extensions, and hook-length formulas
methods: Place the digits into the grid so rows and columns increase; count the linear extensions of the grid poset using the hook-length formula (or a direct recursive/case count), possibly exploiting symmetries of the square.

Reinterpret the condition as a build order on a path graph: each new element must be adjacent in value to an already-placed one, so count orderings by tracking the set of placed values as an interval that grows one step left or right from the start.

Model valid orderings as linear extensions of a graph built on consecutive-integer adjacency; count by tracking the contiguous interval of already-placed values and counting the available boundary choices at each step via a recurrence/DP.

types.name: matchings and pairings under order or threshold constraints via forced-elimination casework
methods: Count total pairs within each group, subtract sibling pairs, add cross-group handshakes computed by selecting half of the opposite group for each person, then divide by two.
Iterate over which allowed element pairs with the largest remaining value, recursing on the reduced set with memoization.

Determine which large elements can only pair with small ones, count admissible partners for the most constrained large values, subtract the partner figures at risk, then multiply forced free choices and divide for repeated partner options.

types.name: circular seating and cyclic arrangements with adjacency, gap, or opposite-seat constraints
methods: Count total circular seatings divided by symmetry; subtract arrangements where some country's members are isolated from other countries using inclusion-exclusion; reduce fraction.
Place the ambassadors in their allowed alternating seats, treat each advisor as occupying one of the adjacent free seats (resolving conflicts by local casework), then count distinct labeled seatings.
Count total subsets, subtract those with no run of adjacent selected chairs, using the complement of circular binary strings with bounded run length.

types.name: binary strings and sequences with run-length or local adjacency constraints via recurrence/transfer matrix
methods: Characterize when a term becomes zero (a difference vanishes), propagate the recurrence structure over initial triples, and count admissible initial triples by casework.
Parametrize pairs by the position of the first differing bit and count the remaining positions split between ones-bits and zeros-bits, then sum over bit positions.

Fix the constrained day's choice, then count choices for the remaining days by multiplying the available options at each step (each day cannot repeat the previous day's choice), splitting into cases by which side of the fixed day is being filled.

types.name: graph-coloring counts for cycles, posets, and grids via chromatic casework and inclusion-exclusion
methods: Break the cycle by deleting one edge, count valid colorings of the resulting path, then subtract those where the two endpoints share a color to enforce the closing adjacency.

Build the divisibility relation among the integers, split into connected chains and connected components, count proper colorings per chain by fixing the smallest element's color, and multiply over independent components.
Fix a Latin-square-like arrangement of colors so each appears once per row/column, then count valid placements by breaking into cases and using inclusion-exclusion/permutation counting.

types.name: tournament, degree-sequence, orientation, and regular-graph counting via double counting
methods: Count total triples, subtract transitive triples using each vertex's out-degree, and read off the cyclic count.
Enumerate the possible common degree, verify graphicality for each, and count labeled graphs of that degree by classifying by cycle/edge structure.

Model games as edges of a multigraph between the two teams, group edges into rounds so each player plays at most once per round (proper edge coloring / 1-factorization), and count the distinct schedulings, accounting for symmetry.

types.name: Ramsey-type, sum-free, product-free, and forbidden-arithmetic-progression extremal counting
methods: Characterize inscribed rectangles by diametrically opposite pairs; a rectangle occurs exactly when two such opposite-chord pairs share the same color, so a coloring is valid iff no two distinct complementary pairs are both monochromatic of the same color; count colorings by partitioning opposite pairs and applying inclusion-exclusion/binomial enumeration on the number of monochromatic pairs.

Enumerate choices for the two inserted terms subject to the increasing constraints between fixed endpoints; test each candidate against all 4-subsets for arithmetic progression by checking that no equally spaced selection of indices gives equal differences, and count the survivors.

Build a 2-coloring avoiding monochromatic products to get a lower bound, then rule out any such coloring past a threshold by chaining forced colors through overlapping product relations among interval elements.

types.name: pigeonhole guarantees for duplicates, quotas, and bucket sizes
methods: Apply the pigeonhole principle: with k colors, one more than k items forces two items to share a color, so the answer is the number of colors plus one.
Sum the largest safe number of each color (quota minus one, capped by supply), then add one to guarantee the quota.
Divide the count by the number of categories, take the ceiling of the average as the guaranteed minimum.

types.name: probability by complementary counting and restricted sampling without replacement
methods: Count favorable orderings by choosing the block sizes of the two colors, arranging the two blocks, and multiplying by the ways to choose which cards of each color appear; divide by the total ways to choose and order the drawn cards; reduce the fraction.

Count total ways to choose the sample; count the complementary event where all chosen come from different countries (at most one per group) using group sizes; subtract and divide to get the probability, then reduce the fraction.

Let die sizes be m,n; express each sum-count as number of pairs within ranges, impose the ratio and absolute probability equations, reduce to divisibility/divisor constraints on m*n, then minimize m+n over feasible size pairs.

types.name: expected values and order statistics via tail sums and threshold counting
methods: Compute the number of subsets whose least element is at least k using binomial coefficients, sum these counts over k to get the total of all least elements, divide by the total number of subsets, then reduce the fraction.
Count permutations whose minimum occupied diagonal-value exceeds each threshold, use the tail-sum formula for the expected minimum, then reduce the fraction.

types.name: lattice point and lattice path counting under linear, bounded, or obstacle constraints
methods: Count lattice points below the line as a step function of the slope, locate the threshold slopes where the count changes, and subtract consecutive thresholds to get the interval length.

Each path is a monotone staircase from A to B; enumerate the lattice cells/points reachable by such a path whose total length is within the bound, using the fact that the path length equals the Manhattan distance plus twice the number of detours, and count the union of points via row-by-row interval analysis.
Count all monotone lattice paths from start to end; subtract those entering the forbidden square by splitting paths into the first entry point and symmetry/decomposition, using binomial counts.

types.name: geometric incidence counting in the plane or 3D via total-minus-degenerate configurations
methods: Count bounded regions by starting from the many-segment arrangement; use Euler's formula V - E + F = 1 + C, or incrementally add each new segment and add the number of new bounded regions it creates, where that number equals one less than the number of distinct intersection points with existing segments between the lines, summed over all segments, then subtract 1 for the unbounded strip region.
Count all unordered edge pairs, classify into parallel, intersecting, and skew types, determine which types are coplanar, and subtract the non-coplanar (skew) pairs from the total.
count all triples of points, then subtract triples lying on each side by choosing points from each side, and sum

types.name: Burnside/orbit counting for cyclic, rotational, and bracelet symmetries
methods: Enumerate integer side multisets summing to the perimeter, order them cyclically, quotient by rotations (bracelets), then apply the cyclic-quadrilateral existence condition (largest side less than the semiperimeter) to filter valid shapes, and count equivalence classes.

Note that negating all digits maps each representation to the negative of its value; pair representations by sign to count distinct nonnegative values from the total number of digit strings, handling the value zero separately.

Choose total colorings, then count symmetric colorings by pairing cells into rotation orbits: orbits of size 4 contribute equally, orbits of size 1 at the center; sum contributions and divide by total to get the probability.

types.name: compositions and distributions into boxes with capacity or quota constraints
methods: Count total ways to partition textbooks into boxes of the given sizes, then count favorable ways by choosing which box holds all marked items and distributing the rest; divide and reduce.
Choose which guests share a room by partitioning people into singles and pairs, then assign each block (single or pair) to a distinct labeled room, counting the injective placements.
Count nonnegative solutions to the sum-of-parts equation by subtracting 1 from each part, then apply inclusion-exclusion to remove solutions exceeding the upper bound on each part.

types.name: integer partition counting with distinct, bounded, or unordered parts
methods: Set the piles as an increasing triple; count solutions to the sum equation with strict inequalities by substituting offsets to reduce to counting positive solutions without ordering, then divide by symmetry or enforce the ordering directly.

Fix the modal frequency, exclude other values from reaching it, then minimize the count of distinct values by putting as many entries as possible into a few near-maximal non-modal frequencies and checking the remainder.
Set up the number of threes used, require the remaining value to be divisible by two, and count the feasible values of the number of threes.

types.name: binomial-coefficient identities and double-counting/Vandermonde sums
methods: Sum the triple product of binomial coefficients over the triangular index region by recognizing it as a combinatorial convolution identity (Vandermonde-type), reduce to a closed form, then compute the last three digits.

Relate the average count over k-subsets to the total number of k-subsets containing a team; the averages become m*C(n-5,k-5)/C(n,k). Set the 9-subset average equal to the reciprocal of the 8-subset average, simplify, and count feasible n in the range.
Double count the sum by fixing each element and counting pairs where it lies in both subsets, then evaluate the resulting binomial sums using the Vandermonde identity and simplify the ratio.

types.name: 0-1 matrices and assignment tables with prescribed row/column sums
methods: Order the row sums and column sums as permutations of 1..n; multiply the number of ways to choose the 1-sets in each row; or use inclusion-exclusion / transfer to count matrices with the given multiset of margins, accounting for symmetry.

Model each department by a selection matrix indexed by gender and department; count valid entries satisfying row sums (gender totals) and column sums (department totals), using casework on how many of each gender come from each department, then multiply department-wise binomial choices and sum over feasible distributions.

types.name: functional-graph, permutation-parity, and determinant counting
methods: Classify by the constant value and number of elements mapping to it; require remaining elements to reach that value in one or two steps, count via rooted-tree/forest structures and inclusion-exclusion.
Reduce to parities; require ad and bc to have opposite parity, split into parity cases, count choices per entry, then add the disjoint cases.

types.name: sieve/elimination survival and periodic-deletion processes
methods: Index the original periodic list by residues, iteratively track which positions survive each sieving step (removing every k-th entry via modular counting), reduce the surviving index to a residue in the pre-erasure list, then read off the digits and sum them.
Simulate repeated passes over the list, removing every other remaining element each pass, and track which position survives.

types.name: rank, median, mode, and committee-total inverse problems
methods: Relate the median rank to the total number of participants n=3k; since the max team rank is below the other two teammates, bound k by the smaller teammate rank; count participants below the median and require exact balance to find k.

Classify which rows contain the middle value and the extremes relative to it, count the ordered arrangements of the remaining values within rows by ordering constraints, and sum over the resulting cases.
Invert the binomial count of the small team to solve for the number of members, then evaluate the binomial count of the larger team with the same total.

types.name: digit-representation optimization and structured-number summation
methods: Express the number in place value by its digit parameters, sum over all allowed digit choices using uniformity of each digit, then extract the digit sum of the total.

Fix the units digits to control the last digit and divisibility by 10; the hundreds contribute a fixed multiple of 100, so minimize by assigning larger digits to tens and smaller to units via rearrangement, with casework on which digits occupy the units positions; then count permutations achieving the minimum and take the absolute difference with the minimum value.

types.name: combinatorial number system and fixed-digit-sum sequence location
methods: Sum block lengths to find which block contains the target position, use triangular-number bounds, then offset within the block.
Compute the binomial coefficient, match its decimal digits against the given pattern, and solve for the repeated digit.
Find the position's binomial decomposition over bit positions, place the required ones in the top bits, add the tail sum of smallest set bits.

types.name: substitution and word-transformation sequences with bounded replacements
methods: Case on the number of substitutions; for k swaps multiply the number of ways to choose on-field players to remove (accounting for earlier substitutes now being eligible) by the number of available substitutes, then sum and reduce modulo.

types.name: absorbing random walks and Hamiltonian-cycle transfer-matrix counts
methods: Model the labeled points as states on two directed cycles joined by spokes; set up a transfer matrix or recurrence tracking the position, iterate the recurrence for the required number of steps to count return paths, then reduce modulo 1000.

Model positions as vertices of a toroidal grid with steps moving one coordinate; count directed Hamiltonian cycles through the origin by turning them into spanning-tree-type structures or via transfer-matrix/number-theoretic decomposition, then reduce modulo 1000.
Set up recurrences for the number of walks from each vertex to the absorbing vertex by length, using symmetry to collapse states, then sum counts over lengths up to the bound.

types.name: set triples with prescribed intersection patterns via membership classification
methods: Classify squares by position symmetry; determine which neighbor sets can produce the required target via casework on boundary and corner cells; count valid initial states.

Classify each element by which of A, B, C it belongs to, enumerate allowed membership patterns subject to pairwise intersections and empty triple intersection, count independent assignments per element, then subtract/correct for overcounting arising from the exact-pairwise-intersection constraints by focusing on the three distinguished shared elements.

types.name: geometric probability from area/volume of a favorable region
methods: Set up the favorable region in the cube by ordering the variables and imposing separation inequalities, compute its volume by inclusion-exclusion/translation, then solve the resulting inequality for the smallest integer parameter.

Compute the probability as the integral over the region of the measure of points whose midpoint with a given point lies in the region, normalized by the square of the area; exploit symmetry and split into cases to evaluate.

Model sample space as product of perimeter segments, find region where distance is below the threshold by splitting cases on which sides the points lie, compute the area/measure of the near region using integrals or circle geometry, subtract from total measure to get the probability.

types.name: random-walk hitting/absorption probability via reflection, symmetry, and Markov recursion
methods: Set up a recurrence for the probability of ever reaching the target from each state; solve the recurrence by complementary counts or a second-order linear recurrence, then reduce the resulting fraction.

Model each frog's position as an independent walk on the cycle; by rotation symmetry reduce to the separations between frogs, or equivalently track the list of pairwise differences. Set up first-step equations for the expected absorption time from each state of the relative-position chain, apply the symmetry of the initial configuration to cut the state space, and solve the resulting linear system for the expected hitting time.

Count total paths; subtract paths that never reach the level by reflecting about the forbidden level, or use the ballot/reflection argument to count hitting paths, then reduce the fraction and sum numerator and denominator.

types.name: conditional probability / Bayes update from weighted or Venn-region counts
methods: Let the Saturday probability be given; set up the conditional Sunday probability as a ratio unknown, use total probability for Sunday to solve the unknown, then compute the union probability via inclusion-exclusion.

Multiply each group's population share by its take-rate to get each group's contribution, sum for the total, divide the target group's contribution by the total, then reduce and sum numerator and denominator.
Use Bayes' rule to get the posterior over which die was chosen from the likelihoods of the observed rolls, then average the third-roll probability over the posterior.

types.name: combinatorial probability via counting, inclusion-exclusion, and no-replacement pairing
methods: Count ordered pairs of distinct gates; count pairs within the distance threshold by fixing the first gate and summing allowed second choices; form reduced fraction and add numerator and denominator.
Compute probabilities of not matching on earlier rounds and then matching on the target round by tracking the number of colors remaining with both socks present, updating after each draw.

Model each person's placement as a random permutation; compute probability no box is monochromatic by inclusion-exclusion over the set of monochromatic-color matching events, counting compatible permutation tuples, then subtract from 1 and reduce the resulting fraction.

types.name: sequential independent trials: success or stopping probability from complements, products, and state recursion
methods: Compute the single-trial success probability, use complementation so the probability of at least one success is one minus the no-success probability raised to the number of trials, then solve the resulting inequality for the smallest integer number of trials.

Write the probability of first stopping at step n as the product of surviving the earlier boxes and failing at the nth; compare the resulting product against the given threshold and find the least index by monotonicity/bounds.
Find the probability a single coin is heads after repeated tossing, then multiply by the number of coins by linearity of expectation.

types.name: distribution of a sum of independent discrete random variables via symmetry or convolution
methods: Use the symmetric transformation of each die value about its mean to pair sums equidistant from the total mean, so the two sums have equal probability.
Compute each player's distribution of heads, then sum the squares of the probabilities over the possible head counts.
Normalize the weights into probabilities, convolve the two independent distributions over pairs summing to the target, sum the products, and reduce the resulting fraction.

types.name: measurement uncertainty: error propagation and sample-size/precision scaling
methods: Sum counts over many independent equal-length intervals; the total is Poisson with mean equal to the number of intervals times the mean per interval, so the relative uncertainty scales as one over the square root of the total count. Set the relative uncertainty equal to the target and solve for the number of intervals.

Compute each combined uncertainty by propagating the individual uncertainties (quadrature for the simple average, inverse-variance weighting for the weighted average) and rank the resulting uncertainties.

Model the per-coin weights as independent identically distributed variables; the estimate of the total has relative uncertainty determined by the per-coin uncertainty divided by the square root of the sample size and scaled by the population-to-sample ratio, then solve for the sample size that meets the target relative uncertainty.

types.name: tournament bracket probability via path enumeration and pairwise win probabilities
methods: Enumerate the possible final opponents by conditioning on the other semifinal winner; multiply each path's match win probabilities and sum the disjoint cases.
Enumerate the equally likely semifinal pairings, compute each player's wins through semis and final using independence, and average the probabilities.

types.name: descriptive statistics: outlier count via IQR fences
methods: Compute the interquartile range, form the lower and upper outlier fences by adding/subtracting 1.5 times the IQR to the quartiles, then count data values falling outside the fences.

types.name: kinematics with constant acceleration
methods: Use free-fall distance proportional to time squared; set each weight's height proportional to the square of a rank index so successive impacts occur at equal time intervals.
Use v^2 = u^2 - 2ad with fixed distance d and deceleration a; compare the two cases to solve for the unknown impact speed.
Set the radial velocity to zero to find the time or position of closest/farthest approach, then evaluate position magnitude at that instant.

types.name: velocity-time graph interpretation
methods: Read peak velocity values off each velocity-time graph, compare magnitudes, and order them.
Identify downward velocity as the negative-most value; find the time interval where the velocity-time curve is at its lowest constant level.
Read initial and final velocities from each graph over the interval, compute the change in velocity divided by the time interval for each, compare the magnitudes, and rank them.

types.name: projectile motion
methods: Use vertical kinematics to get max height from initial vertical velocity, use horizontal kinematics over total flight time to get range, then form the ratio and simplify using the launch angle.

Rotate to coordinates aligned with the incline so bounces become simple reflections of the velocity normal component; use the periodic straight-line motion in the rotated frame to impose that the trajectory returns to the starting point after two bounces, then solve the resulting trigonometric condition for the launch angle.
Write height as a function of angle using the horizontal-distance constraint, differentiate, and solve the resulting trigonometric equation for the extremal angle.

types.name: relative velocity and river crossing
methods: Find the boat's cross-river velocity component by subtracting the current from the resultant straight-across velocity using the Pythagorean relation, then divide the river width by that component.

Use momentum conservation and energy conservation in the ground frame; relate the puck's velocity relative to the wedge to its ground-frame velocity via vector velocity addition, then solve for the puck's speed on the horizontal surface.

Use conservation of energy in the ramp frame to get the speed at the bottom; then transform the velocity to the ground frame by adding the ramp's velocity vector, and compute the resulting kinetic energy.

types.name: constraint kinematics (sliding rods, geometry)
methods: Write both endpoint velocity components in terms of angular rate, express midpoint as average of endpoints, then eliminate angular rate using the given endpoint speed.

Use energy conservation to get speed at each height; resolve velocity into tangential and component directions, diagnose monotonicity of speed, horizontal component, and vertical component separately using symmetry/geometry of the path.
Relate the two endpoint velocities by projecting the rod's velocity constraint along the rod (fixed length), using the angles of the rod with each surface to get the ratio of speeds.

types.name: work-energy theorem
methods: Differentiate the potential with respect to position and take the negative to obtain the force.

Compute the net work as the sum of the applied-force work, gravity work, and friction work over the displacement along the ramp; set equal to the change in kinetic energy from rest and solve for the final speed.
Use work-energy theorem: the braking force acting through the stopping distance equals the initial kinetic energy; also relate to power times time using constant speed relations.

types.name: power and drag-limited motion
methods: Write instantaneous relative speed as mean plus fluctuation, express dissipation rate, average, compare mean of square to square of mean using the fluctuation's variance to decide sign.

Express power output as proportional to mass; express drag power as proportional to area times speed cubed; relate area to mass using constant density and the cube shape; set power equal to drag power and solve for the speed-mass proportionality exponent.
Set engine power equal to the rate of work done against the net resisting force; compute force times speed, using the given force law.

types.name: motion with air drag
methods: Set up Newton's second law with drag opposing velocity; on the way up, both gravity and drag decelerate so the slope is steep and the velocity reaches zero in finite time; on the way down, drag opposes gravity so acceleration shrinks toward zero and velocity approaches terminal velocity with decreasing slope.

Set up the vertical equation of motion including the drag component along the vertical direction, noting the drag term depends on speed (hence on horizontal velocity for linear drag); compare the vertical dynamics of the two objects and determine whether horizontal motion influences the vertical fall time, for both drag laws.

Apply Newton's second law with gravity and a velocity-opposing drag force; the acceleration is directed downward and largest at launch, decreasing in magnitude as the object slows, reaching g at the peak, and continuing downward thereafter.

types.name: momentum and impulse
methods: Compute total momentum from each cart's mass and initial velocity, divide by total mass; since no external force acts, the center-of-mass velocity is unchanged by any collisions.
Use p = mv to relate velocities through equal momentum, then substitute into K = p^2/(2m) (or ½mv²) to express kinetic energy inversely in mass and compare.

Use conservation of momentum to show the momentum change is frame-independent, and transform kinetic energy between frames to see whether its change depends on the reference frame, distinguishing elastic from inelastic cases.

types.name: inelastic collisions and explosions
methods: Set initial momentum equal to final momentum of the combined mass and solve for the common velocity.
Use conservation of momentum to find the common final velocity of the combined mass, then compute the final kinetic energy from the total mass and that velocity.
Conserve linear momentum to find the combined speed right after the clay sticks, then conserve mechanical energy to relate that speed to the maximum height, and convert the height to the swing angle.

types.name: elastic collisions in one dimension
methods: Compute net momentum and check it against each candidate final state; require conservation of momentum and kinetic energy, then reject options that violate either.
Compute total momentum from masses and signed velocities, divide by total mass to get the center-of-mass velocity, noting it is unchanged by the collision.
Apply conservation of momentum and (for elastic case) conservation of kinetic energy to solve for the final velocity of the target ball; use given masses and initial velocities.

types.name: collisions with springs
methods: Find speed of falling mass at impact; use momentum conservation for the perfectly inelastic collision to get velocity of combined mass; track the spring's equilibrium shift; use energy conservation to get maximum compression/displacement amplitude, and add the initial compression offset if needed.
Set equilibrium where spring force balances weight; use energy conservation from collision point to equilibrium point, where speed is maximal, including gravitational potential drop.
Conserve momentum to find common velocity at maximum compression, then equate initial kinetic energy to kinetic plus spring potential energy using the reduced mass.

types.name: collisions with rotation (angular impulse)
methods: Use energy conservation to find the speed just before impact, then impose angular momentum conservation about the pivot to find the resulting angular speed, and relate that to the linear speed of the point of interest.

Compute the rod's moment of inertia about its center of mass, then find the impact height at which the angular impulse about the center equals zero so the rod acquires only linear momentum and no rotation.

Apply linear impulse-momentum to the suspended rod's center of mass and angular impulse-momentum about that center; relate the hinge-end motion to the driving rod's angular velocity via kinematics; eliminate the joint impulse and solve for the ratio of angular speeds.

types.name: rolling without slipping
methods: Compare gravitational potential energy drop to work done against friction; find the angle threshold where friction just sustains rolling without slipping, then evaluate kinetic energy in the rolling and slipping regimes and sketch its dependence on incline angle.

Apply Newton's laws along the incline; relate friction and angular acceleration via rolling constraint; add the shell and fluid moments of inertia (fluid contributes as a non-rotating solid sphere for translational-plus-additional inertia) and solve for acceleration.

Analyze the friction force direction during slipping from the contact-point velocity, apply Newton's second law for translation and rotation to get constant angular acceleration, then set contact-point velocity to zero to find the rolling condition and the resulting final constant angular velocity.

types.name: rotational kinematics
methods: Find times to accelerate and to decelerate from final angular velocity and acceleration; sum the swept angles in those phases and in the constant-velocity phase to match total angle; solve the remaining constant-rate time and add all phase times.
Relate the synchronous rotation period to the angular speed, then multiply by the radius to get the equatorial surface speed.
Use constant-acceleration rotational kinematics relating angular displacement, initial and final angular velocities; equate the common final/initial speed to solve for the ratio of accelerations.

types.name: angular momentum conservation
methods: Use conservation of angular momentum about the pivot during the instantaneous standing-up (no external torque impulse), relate linear speed of CM to angular speed via the radial distance, set initial and final angular momenta equal, and solve for the relation between the speeds at the two radii.
Identify the system, check external torques about the vertical axis; distinguish the free-flight phase from the collision with the floor where friction/normal force can exert torque.

Use angular momentum conservation to find the new angular speed when the radius shrinks, compute the change in rotational kinetic energy of the system, and equate the work done by the motor to that energy change.

types.name: simple harmonic motion
methods: Identify the period of the motion from the given equation or conditions, then determine the time to first return to the origin as one period (or the appropriate fraction of it).

Find the center of mass by summing spoke moments, compute total moment of inertia about the axle as rim plus rods through an end, then apply the small-oscillation angular frequency formula for a physical pendulum.

Relate original spring constant to the full-length spring; find constant of each half; combine two half springs attached to the mass as parallel springs; insert into angular frequency formula and compare with original.

types.name: pendulum motion
methods: Use the small-angle period proportional to the square root of length to get the leading scaling, then account for the amplitude-dependent correction that always increases the period.

Resolve weight into radial and tangential parts; tangential acceleration points toward equilibrium, radial (centripetal) points toward the pivot; add the two vectors to get the net acceleration direction.

Use the physical pendulum period formula; find moment of inertia about the pivot via parallel-axis theorem (adding the out-of-plane inertia term), then substitute the component of gravity perpendicular to the displacement into the torque and read off the period from small-angle equation of motion.

types.name: coupled oscillators and normal modes
methods: Write the linearized equations of motion, form the matrix of second derivatives, and find its eigenvalues; the physical periodic motion corresponds to the positive eigenvalue, giving the normal-mode frequency and hence the period.

Write Newton's law for each mass under gravity and spring force, subtract the equations to get the relative-coordinate equation of motion, identify the effective mass and spring constant, and read off the period.
Equate total force to sum of each spring's force at the common extension; solve for the equivalent constant and the natural length where net force is zero.

types.name: anharmonic oscillations
methods: Use energy conservation to find allowed region between turning points and the shape/symmetry of oscillations to select the compatible position-time graph.

Write the transverse restoring force as a function of displacement from the geometry of the stretched spring; analyze how the effective stiffness (and thus period) varies with amplitude, taking the small- and large-amplitude limits.

types.name: driven oscillator and resonance
methods: Write the equation of motion in the accelerating frame with effective gravity g plus sinusoidal drive; identify the pendulum's natural frequency and match the drive frequency to it to maximize energy transfer.

types.name: buoyancy and floating
methods: Find block volume from suspended weight and density; compute buoyant force from submerged volume fraction; add buoyant force to water-scale reading and subtract from hanging-scale reading.

Set up equilibrium in the accelerating frame with effective gravity equal to g plus the upward acceleration, equate buoyant force to the block's weight, solve for the submerged volume fraction, and compare with the original density ratio to determine whether the block sinks or rises.

Use Archimedes' principle (buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid), relate displaced volume to pressure via Boyle's law, and note pressure increases with depth so volume decreases, then compare forces at the two depths.

types.name: hydrostatics
methods: Set pressures equal at the base of the tube; express each column's pressure as density times column length; impose equal oil and water lengths and solve for the height difference in terms of the common length.
Use F = (pressure at base) × (base area), equate the pressure to the water column height (depth) times density times gravity, and relate each flask's water height to its shape given equal volume.

Seal the hemispheres at low internal pressure, return to higher ambient pressure; find the net inward force on one hemisphere as the pressure difference times the projected circular area, then set the required pulling force equal to that net force.

types.name: fluid dynamics
methods: Find each pipe's speed from its filling rate and cross-section, then subtract the two speeds to get the difference.
Use continuity to relate the piston and exit speeds through the area ratio, apply Bernoulli to get the pressure difference, then multiply by the piston area to obtain the force.

Apply continuity to find speeds in each section from the area ratio and total flow, then use Bernoulli's equation to relate the pressure difference between sections, converting pressure difference to a water-column height difference.

types.name: orbital mechanics
methods: Relate total energy to kinetic energy for a circular orbit (virial theorem), then determine the change in kinetic energy from the given change in total energy.

A rigid body rotates with all layers sharing the same angular velocity, so linear speed is proportional to radius. Independently orbiting particles follow gravitational centripetal balance, so speed squared is inversely proportional to orbital radius. Compare each given scaling to these two laws to decide whether the layer belongs to the planet or to the satellites.

Set centripetal force equal to gravitational force for a circular orbit, solve for enclosed mass as speed squared times radius over G, then read the shape of the speed curve to determine how enclosed mass grows with radius.

types.name: gravitation: escape velocity and field
methods: Set kinetic energy equal to gravitational potential energy difference, use surface gravity relation to eliminate mass, and solve for speed.
Integrate contributions from thin circular rings; use symmetry to cancel horizontal components and integrate the axial component over the polar angle to find the net force.
Set energy at launch equal to energy at the saddle point where net gravitational force vanishes; solve the resulting potential-energy equation for the minimum speed.

types.name: central force motion
methods: Use conservation of energy and angular momentum; evaluate radial effective potential at the closest-approach point to determine whether the motion is bounded or unbounded, then infer the long-time asymptotics of the trajectory.

Consider a test particle on a shell; only the mass interior to its radius acts (shell theorem). Write its equation of motion, parametrize the orbit with a cycloid, and integrate from rest to singularity to get the collapse time in terms of initial density and radius.

types.name: static equilibrium (torques, trusses, tipping)
methods: Place the pivot as origin, treat the rod's weight as acting at its geometric center, set the sum of torques from the rod and the added mass equal (one on each side), and solve for the rod mass.

Find the tipping axis through the relevant pair of support points, compute the moment arm from the center of mass to this axis from the polygon geometry, then equate the applied-force torque about the pivot to the restoring gravitational torque and solve for the minimum force.

Treat block+wedge as one system; the only external horizontal force on it is the ground friction, and the block's weight contributes no net external horizontal force, so balance horizontal external forces to find the ground friction magnitude.

types.name: friction (static/kinetic, thresholds)
methods: Determine whether the friction needed for rolling exceeds the static maximum; if so the sphere slips and kinetic friction does negative work, reducing final kinetic energy, otherwise energy is conserved; compare the friction threshold angle to the choices to find which conserves the most energy.

Relate hoop tension to radial normal force per unit length (curved band pressure), integrate around the contact to get total normal force, set limiting friction equal to the band's weight, and solve for the friction coefficient.
Relate the maximum spring force to the amplitude, set it equal to the limiting static friction on the platform, and solve for the maximum initial speed from energy conservation.

types.name: pulley systems and constraints
methods: Set up tension equations for each hanging mass, relate rope accelerations through the common angular acceleration of the two cylinders, apply torque balance on the massless cylinders to eliminate tension and angular acceleration, then form the ratio of the net forces.

Write force balance at each pulley and the hanging mass to get spring tensions in terms of weight; use Hooke's law for each spring's stretch; apply the kinematic constraint linking rope-end displacement to spring-length changes through the pulley geometry; subtract the two equilibrium configurations.

Write Newton's equations for each mass, combine to get acceleration in terms of the masses, then substitute into the tension expression and take the limit of the mass ratio to determine the asymptotic behavior.

types.name: non-inertial frames
methods: Switch to the box frame, add the pseudo-force from the box acceleration, note it shifts the equilibrium while the spring dynamics (period, relative oscillation) are unaffected; compare each listed quantity to the inertial-frame values at release.
Resolve tension into vertical and horizontal components; set vertical balance against weight and horizontal balance against pseudo-force, then divide to eliminate tension and solve for acceleration.
Go to the freely falling frame, show gravity is canceled by the frame's fictitious force, conclude the restoring force and effective gravity are unchanged, so the angular frequency stays the same.

types.name: rotating frame equilibrium
methods: Compare the jumper's conserved angular momentum with the ground's as the jump height increases the distance from Earth's axis; compute the horizontal drift over the flight time and eliminate flight time in favor of jump height.
Set up forces in the rotating frame: centripetal requirement equals the net spring force from both springs, using each spring's extension from its relaxed length; solve for the equilibrium radius.
Set spring extension from the rest length, equate the net inward spring force component to the centripetal force needed for circular motion at the given radius, and solve for the spring constant.

types.name: dimensional analysis
methods: Write dimensions of each quantity, assume a power-law product equals a dimensionless constant, solve the exponent equations, then match against the answer choices.
Use the drag force law and dimensional analysis to find how force scales with density, length, and velocity; equate the forces for the two bodies and solve for the unknown velocity.
Use dimensional analysis to find how drag force depends on length, speed, and viscosity via the only dimensionless combination, then set drag force equal for equal thrust and solve the speed ratio.

types.name: error propagation
methods: Use the pendulum formula to express g in terms of L and T, compute the central value, then combine the fractional uncertainties (with the exponent on T) in quadrature to get the absolute uncertainty.
Differentiate or use relative errors of the formula for the derived quantity and combine them in quadrature to get the absolute uncertainty.

Compute the spring constant from measured elongation, mass, and gravity; find fractional uncertainties from ruler precision, scale discrepancy, and stated g uncertainty; combine in quadrature (or sum relative errors) to get percent error.

types.name: elasticity and stress
methods: Compute rod cross-sectional area from diameter, multiply by tensile strength to get maximum force, then divide by gravitational acceleration to get mass.
Recognize equal opposite pulls produce a tension equal to one force; apply Hooke's law to find extension and add to equilibrium length.

Use Hooke's law to express tension in terms of extension, take wave speed proportional to square root of tension, compute travel time as length divided by speed, and compare the two stretch configurations.

types.name: waves on strings and rings
methods: Relate fundamental frequency to wave speed and fixed string length; express linear mass density through cross-sectional area and material density; determine maximum tension from breaking stress times cross-sectional area; form the ratio and simplify.
Relate wave speed to tension and linear density; set centripetal tension proportional to omega squared; compare speeds between the two rotation rates.

types.name: circular motion (banking, vertical circles)
methods: Balance vertical tension against weight and horizontal tension against centripetal force to get the cone angle via tan theta = v^2/(rg); then find the height difference from the rope length times cosine of that angle.
Set centripetal acceleration equal to the tolerance limit to find the speed; multiply mass times speed times radius to get angular momentum.

Relate spring constant to the change in circumference (tension proportional to strain times original length), equate the radial component of hoop tension to the centripetal force per unit length of the rotating band, and solve for the new radius.

types.name: kinetic theory and pressure from momentum flux
methods: Express pressure as force per area from the momentum delivered per unit time by drops hitting the ground; mass per drop scales as radius cubed, so pressure scales as number density times radius cubed times speed squared; apply the changes to each factor and multiply.

types.name: variable mass systems
methods: Compute the total kinetic energy as a function of time using the growing mass, then differentiate with respect to time; combine with the mass accumulation rate.

types.name: two-body dynamics (center of mass, reduced mass)
methods: Equate gravitational force to centripetal force for each mass, use equal angular velocity and center-of-mass relation to get speed ratio inversely proportional to mass ratio.

Compute gravitational force from the product of masses at fixed separation; compute total angular momentum via reduced mass and center-of-mass orbital speed; check how each quantity changes when mass is transferred at fixed separation.
Use conservation of linear momentum and energy in the center-of-mass frame; find the constant angular speed of the point mass relative to the ring; period is one full relative revolution.

types.name: surface tension and bubble pressure
methods: Compare internal pressures via the pressure-radius relation, identify which bubble has higher pressure, then determine the direction of air flow through the connecting bridge to find the final state.

Compute surface area change of two drops merging into one (surface energy released proportional to r^2); set equal to gravitational potential energy of the merged drop, which depends on its radius; solve for height scaling with r.
Recognize mass/volume is conserved (no evaporation), then compare areas: the sphere minimizes surface area for given volume, so splitting a cylinder into droplets increases total surface area.

types.name: adiabatic invariants and slow changes
methods: Use the adiabatic invariant that speed times separation is constant; compare the initial product of speed and gap to the final product when the gap has shrunk, and solve for the final speed.

Use conservation of the adiabatic invariant (angular momentum or action) as the central mass changes slowly; relate circular-orbit radius to the mass using the invariant, then compute the fractional change.

Count time spent at each position from simple harmonic motion; multiply by constant leak rate to get water deposited per position; note bucket lowers as water drains, using conservation of angular momentum to shorten the effective length and speed up the swing.

types.name: tidal forces and gravity-gradient
methods: Compare gravitational forces on the two masses (differential gravity) and centripetal requirements in the co-rotating frame to find the rod force (tension vs compression); then evaluate the tidal torque on a tilted dumbbell to determine whether the radial orientation is stable, unstable, or neutral.

types.name: charged particle in uniform fields
methods: Determine the net force from electric and magnetic fields, resolve into components along and perpendicular to the field, and match the resulting trajectory (parabolic drift plus circular motion) to the given path shapes.

types.name: moment of inertia (composite bodies)
methods: Find the moment of inertia about the pivot for each oscillation direction, form the equation of motion for small angular displacements, and take the ratio of the resulting periods.
Decompose the plate into thin strips parallel to the axis, compute each strip's inertia with the parallel-axis theorem, and integrate over the strip position.

Decompose the figure into congruent triangular pieces sharing the axis, apply parallel-axis theorem to shift each piece's known centroidal inertia to the required axis, and sum the contributions scaled by mass.

types.name: rigid body dynamics (pivoting, lifting)
methods: Use conservation of linear momentum to find the constant COM velocity; use conservation of angular momentum about the COM to find the angular velocity; the velocity of the second mass is the COM velocity plus its rotational velocity, set it to zero and solve the resulting trigonometric equation for the time.

Resolve the impulse into components along and perpendicular to the rod; the perpendicular component drives uniform circular motion about the vertical rod axis, then use circumference over speed to find the period.

Write Newton's second law for the center-of-mass acceleration, then take torque about the center of mass to relate the ground normal force to the applied end force, and combine with the force equation to solve for the normal force.

types.name: collisions in two dimensions
methods: Apply momentum conservation in both axes and kinetic energy conservation for the equal-mass elastic collision, compute the center-of-mass velocity from momentum over total mass, and check each statement against these results to find the one that need not hold.
Apply conservation of momentum in two directions and conservation of kinetic energy, then solve the resulting system for the unknown final speeds.
